title: They Asked Me Why I Wrote No Elegy for My Father
intro: Ahmad Shawqi's elegy for his father, Ali Bey Shawqi, stands in the third part of al-Shawqiyyat, his collected poems, among the elegies, under the heading “He mourns his father”; a note there says he wrote it around 1897, and Shawqi Dayf dates the father's death to 1895. It opens by answering those who asked why he had written no elegy for his father and by recalling that every soul must die. This recitation begins with the next lines, on death's reach, which spares neither eagle nor lion; he and his father, he says, were one soul, so that each has met death twice; parents in general are mercy itself; he remembers the table, the vessel and the walks they shared, and ends with questions to his father about the hour of his death, about meeting again, and about whether they will lie in one grave or two. The recitation leaves out the poem's first six lines and two others, and repeats the last. Two critics read it in opposite ways: Shawqi Dayf thought it “perhaps the finest of Shawqi's elegies”, because it “came from his heart”, and elsewhere quotes its lines on father and son among elegies that “drip with grief and sorrow, longing and anguish”, while Muhammad al-Majdhub calls “I am the one who died” and the line after it a “cold philosophising” that makes Shawqi forget to describe his grief.

translation: Death has a hand that, when it strikes,
could all but split the two Farqad stars apart.
1.sharh: Nothing escapes death's reach: its blow could nearly part the Farqadan, the two stars that Arabic proverb makes the image of inseparable companions. No bond is too old or too close for it.

translation: It pierces the sky to reach its eagles,
and meets the lion between the two mountains.
2.sharh: Death's hand goes everywhere: high in the air it overtakes the eagles that rule the sky, and on the ground it confronts the lion in the mountains. Neither height nor strength is a refuge.

translation: I am the one who died, and the one who died is I:
each of us has met death twice.
3.sharh: Father and son are one being, so each death is both of theirs and each meets death twice. Though no commentator says so, this line and the next recall al-Hallaj's “I am the one I love”, whose lovers are “two spirits in one body”; here they are one spirit in two.

translation: We were one soul in a single body,
then we became one soul in two bodies.
4.sharh: Before the son was born he was part of his father, one life in one body; at his birth that life came to live in two bodies. The son is his father continued, not another person.

translation: Then we were one soul in one body again,
then we shall be laid out, one corpse in two shrouds.
5.sharh: When the father died he left his soul in his son, so they were one soul in one body again. When the son dies, the two will be a single dead man in two shrouds.

translation: Look at the world and say, describing it:
all this comes from two parents.
6.sharh: He turns from his own father to parents in general. Everyone in the world goes back to a single pair, Adam and Eve in al-Abyari's reading, so parenthood is the root from which all mankind grows.

translation: And if someone asks what those two are made of,
say: they are mercy, in two shapes of mercy.
7.sharh: If asked what parents are, answer that they are mercy itself, embodied twice over, once in the father and once in the mother. Having made parents the root of mankind, he makes mercy the root of parents.

translation: They lost the Garden to bring us into being,
and through them we have enjoyed two gardens.
8.sharh: Adam and Eve gave up paradise so that we could exist, since in paradise they would have had no children on earth. Through them we gain two gardens: this world's good things and paradise in the next.

translation: They are our excuse when they are angered,
and our pardon when we seek to please them.
9.sharh: When their children anger them, parents make the excuse for them themselves; when the children ask to be forgiven, they forgive at once. They are not merely forgiving: they are forgiveness itself.

translation: I wonder which living soul has not held
the faith those two held at the very beginning.
10.sharh: No one alive fails to hold the faith his first parents held: al-Abyari takes it as belief in God, inherited from Adam and Eve. It can also mean that every child first takes the religion of his own parents.

translation: God has stopped us where they stand,
and let the messengers die, all but our parents.
11.sharh: We stay where our parents stand and keep their ways. The prophets are dead and their mission ended, but parents remain messengers whose message never ends, shaping their children in their own image, as the note in al-Shawqiyyat explains.

translation: My father was nothing but a brother I have lost:
his love was truth, and people's love is a lie.
12.sharh: His father was a brother, never a master, and his love was true where other people's is false. The note in al-Shawqiyyat calls this simple line his highest praise of his father, since such a father has every virtue.

translation: How often we sat down together at a table
where a single crust became two.
13.sharh: Father and son ate at one table and split every piece of bread between them, half each, as al-Abyari explains. Nothing was the father's alone; they shared as equals.

translation: We drank from a single vessel,
and afterwards washed our hands in it.
14.sharh: They drank from one vessel and afterwards washed their hands in it. Such small daily things show father and son living side by side as companions, not as a master and his charge.

translation: We walked about, my hand in his;
whoever saw us said we were brothers.
15.sharh: They walked hand in hand, and strangers took them for two brothers rather than father and son. What others saw bears out what he said a few lines earlier, that his father was a brother to him.

translation: Fate cast a single look at us,
a look that dealt out harm equally, and so it was two looks.
16.sharh: When fate turned its eye on them, one glance struck both alike: whatever harm fell on the father fell on the son, as al-Abyari explains. So one blow counts double, as each of them met death twice.

translation: Father, death is a bitter cup
that no soul tastes twice.
17.sharh: Death is a bitter drink that each person tastes only once, so only those who have drunk it know what it is like, and they cannot come back to tell. So he must ask his father.

translation: What was it like, that hour you went through,
beside which all that comes before or after is easy?
18.sharh: He asks his father about the hour of his death, so hard that every hardship before it, and whatever comes after, seems light beside it. A son wants to share even this with his father.

translation: Did you drink death there in a single gulp,
or did you drink it in two?
19.sharh: Keeping to the image of the cup, he asks whether death came to his father quickly, in one swallow, or slowly and painfully, in two.

translation: Do not fear grief or weeping after you are gone:
today an eye, both mine and yours, has frozen.
20.sharh: He tells his dead father not to fear that grief and tears will overwhelm him. The eye they share is dry: the father's in death, the son's in the patience his father taught him.

translation: It was you who taught me to give up grief:
every beauty that ends in death is a blemish.
21.sharh: His father taught him not to grieve. Whatever is lovely in this world ends in death, and so its loveliness is a flaw: nothing that must be lost is worth mourning.

translation: I wish I knew: may we meet
once more, or is this the parting of night and day?
22.sharh: He wonders whether he will ever meet his father again, or whether they are parted like night and day, which follow each other for ever but never meet, unlike the inseparable Farqad stars of the opening.

translation: And when I die and am laid in the earth,
shall we be given one pit, or two?
23.sharh: His last question is whether, when he too is buried, father and son will share one grave or lie in two. It returns to the image of one corpse in two shrouds, as if he hoped one grave would hold them as one soul did.

1.2.4.head: الفَرقَدان
1.2.4.meaning: Al-Farqadan: two stars near the celestial pole that circle together and never set; Arabs say “longer in company than the two Farqads”.

4.1.3.head: مُهجَة
4.1.3.meaning: Muhja: the soul, the life; also blood.

10.1.1-2.meaning: “Would that my knowledge”: I wish I knew.

10.1.6.head: دانَ
10.1.6.meaning: Holds as one's faith; al-Abyari glosses it “believe”.

16.1.2.head: الدَّهر
16.1.2.meaning: Dahr: time, fate, which Arabic poets blame for every misfortune.

18.2.6.meaning: Easy, light; a shortened form of hayyin.

22.2.5.head: المَلَوان
22.2.5.meaning: Al-Malawan: the two times, night and day, or, some say, the two ends of the day.

23.1.2.head: ماتَ
23.1.2.meaning: I die: the reciter says muttu; al-Abyari prints mittu, the other form of the word.

23.2.1.head: لَقّى
23.2.1.meaning: Shall we be given: the passive of laqqa, to give or present someone with something, as in the Quran's “none is given it but those who are patient” (41:35).

23.2.3.meaning: Or: so the reciter says; the editions have am, the “or” that asks which of two things is so.
